en: Wearing a mask during the dusty Ati-Atihan festival protects your lungs from inhaling harmful street smoke and ash.
Fermenting fish to make bagoong produces lactic acid that blocks harmful bacteria, keeping the traditional food safe to eat.
Ifugao rice terraces use stone-walled steps to slow water runoff, preventing soil erosion and deadly landslides during heavy typhoons.
Hero Jose Rizal studied ophthalmology in Europe to successfully treat his mother’s cataracts and restore her failing vision.
The Department of Health enforces clean air rules to reduce vehicle smoke, protecting citizens from severe respiratory diseases.
Practicing bayanihan to clean neighborhood drainage canals before the rainy season prevents dengue-carrying mosquitoes from breeding in stagnant water.
Filipino scientist Dr. Fe del Mundo invented a bamboo incubator to safely keep premature babies warm in rural areas without electricity.
Protecting the Philippine eagle's large forest habitat also preserves vital watersheds that supply clean drinking water to nearby communities.
Indigenous Aeta people used their traditional knowledge of volcanic ash to safely guide evacuees away from deadly mudflows during the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption.
The Constitution guarantees the right to a healthful ecology, empowering citizens to report illegal logging that worsens harmful community flooding.
During the MassKara Festival, wearing breathable masks over elaborate face paint prevents skin irritation and allows safe breathing while dancing in the heat.
Filipino families traditionally use calamansi, a native citrus fruit rich in vitamin C, to naturally boost the immune system against common colds.
